title: The withered hand (Mark 3:1–6)
hookLine: he looks around in anger at hard hearts, and heals on the sabbath anyway

lines: A MAN WITH A WITHERED HAND.
cards: A meeting where everyone is waiting to see which side someone will take: that's the mood in this synagogue, on a sabbath. Jesus walks in, and there's a man whose hand is withered, shrunken and useless.
Mark says some people there are watching Jesus, not the man, to see whether he'll heal on the sabbath, so they'll have something against him. The man has become a test case. Jesus knows it.
The whole room knows it. And Mark says what Jesus felt.

teach.b: Jesus doesn't do it quietly in a corner. He tells the man, stand up in the middle.

teach.h: TO SAVE LIFE, OR TO KILL?
teach.b: Then he turns to the room, in the King James Bible: "Is it lawful to do good on the sabbath days, or to do evil? to save life, or to kill?" It's a question with only one decent answer. "But they held their peace."

Then comes the verse Mark keeps and the other gospels soften: "when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand."

Anger and grief in the same breath. Hardness here is a word for skin gone thick and stiff, like a callus: a heart that can't feel anymore. The man stretches out his hand, and it's restored, whole as the other.
Jesus doesn't touch him. He just asks him to do the one thing his hand couldn't: reach. And the ending is dark.
Some Pharisees go out and start planning with supporters of King Herod how to destroy Jesus. Three chapters in, and already there's a plot. Readers take a few things from this.
That doing good is never out of season.

teach.h: ANGER AND GRIEF AT HARD HEARTS.
teach.b: That Jesus's anger is real, and aimed at hard hearts, not at hurting people.
And that sometimes the healing starts when someone asks you to stretch toward what you think you can't do.

how: Many Christians read this passage as a call to do good without waiting for the convenient moment, and churches often hold healing services or pray for the sick with hands outstretched or laid on them.

o: toughness that helps you endure hard times
strict obedience to every rule of the law
a heart gone stiff, like a callus, unable to feel

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: anger and grief at hard hearts

s: Jesus touched the man's hand to heal it
he didn't touch him. he told him to stretch it out, and it was restored.
Mark is the gospel that tells us Jesus looked around in anger
the other gospels tell the story but soften or leave out the anger.
after this healing, everyone in the room rejoiced
some went out and began to plot against him with Herod's supporters.

games.q: you're Jesus. a room is watching to see if you'll heal a man on the sabbath so they can accuse you. what do you do?
o: wait until tomorrow and heal him then.
call him into the middle and heal him now.
heal him quietly after the crowd leaves.
games.why: he calls the man to stand in the middle, asks whether it's lawful to do good or evil, and heals him in front of everyone.

practice: Hold one hand out in front of you, palm open, and feel the small effort of reaching.

Think of a good thing you've been putting off because it would be awkward, thanking someone out loud, speaking up in a meeting for someone who's being talked over, checking on a person after a hard conversation, and picture yourself doing it, awkwardness and all.
If you pray, open your hand to God; then let it rest.

wordCard.voice: Hardness, the callused heart Jesus grieved over in the watching room, right before he told the man to stretch out his hand.

orig.note: Greek: a hardening, like a callus. Mark's word for the hardness of their hearts.

carryVoice: Your line: stretch out your hand. Doing good is never out of season. That's day one hundred sixty-seven.
